sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Ask a man what it means to be blessed and watch how quickly his eyes go to his circumstances. The raise. The clean scan. The house that finally sold. The son who came home. You have been trained by a hundred quiet sermons — most of them not preached from any pulpit — to read the word blessed as a scoreboard, and to check the scoreboard every morning to see where you stand with God.

That reading will crush you. Not immediately, and not all at once, but eventually and completely, because the scoreboard turns. It always turns. And when it does, a man who has learned to measure God’s favor by his circumstances will conclude the one thing Ephesians was written to make impossible: that God has withdrawn.

The dust says your standing with God is a variable — that it rises when the quarter is good and falls when the diagnosis comes, that blessing is something God is currently deciding about you based on the last few weeks. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has believed that and gone face-down under it: my soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)
And the reviving word of Ephesians 1 is that God’s blessing of you was finished before the world had a surface for dust to settle on.

sections.heading: A Letter About the Church, Written to Men in Trouble
pulls: The dust says your standing with God rises and falls with your week. Ephesians 1 says the blessing was settled before the foundation of the world — and a blessing that early cannot be undone by a bad Tuesday.
paras: No book in the Bible explains the church more thoroughly than Ephesians. Paul writes to show that the church is the community in which God reconciles sinners to Himself and then remakes them into His image — and he writes it from a prison cell, to a congregation under pressure, in a city whose trade was bound up with the worship of another god entirely.

So the blessings he begins with are not the kind that can be confiscated. They do not come as property, position, or relief. They are spiritual, heavenly, and permanent — things the world did not supply and the thief cannot reach. Before you go further, read the whole letter through in one sitting. It is six short chapters, and reading them together will keep you from mistaking the parts for the whole.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: BLESSED IN THE HEAVENLY PLACES
paras: Watch the direction of the first sentence. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us. Paul blesses God because God has blessed us — and the two verbs are not the same act. When God blesses, He confers. When you bless Him, you acknowledge. You have nothing to give Him that He did not first give you.

And the location matters. Every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. That phrase runs through this letter like a thread; Paul will use it again to say where Christ is seated, where you are seated with Him, and where the war is being fought. It is not a description of the sky. It is the place where the decisive things about your life are settled — which is precisely why your blessings are still intact after the year you have had.

So what are they? Paul lists them the way a man reads out an inventory already signed for: chosen, predestined, adopted, favored, redeemed, forgiven, lavished upon, let in on the secret. Not offers. Holdings.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: CHOSEN BEFORE THE FOUNDATION
paras: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love. Sit with the timestamp. Before Adam, before the garden, before there was a single soul in need of saving, God had set His love on you and determined to have you.

What that means is that your salvation was never an afterthought with God. It was forethought. Your redemption was not His improvised response to a crisis He did not see coming; it was the outworking of a purpose He held before He said let there be light. Nothing about you surprised Him into loving you, which means nothing about you can surprise Him out of it.

And notice the purpose clause, because men skip it: He chose us that we would be holy and without defect before him in love. Election is not a hammock. It tells a man what he was chosen for. God did not choose you so you could stay as you are — and He chose you in love, which is the only atmosphere in which a man can be told the truth about himself and survive it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ADOPTED, AND AT WHAT PRICE
pulls: No man is able to deal with the problem and the consequences of his own sin. He requires rescue from outside himself. That rescue has a price, and the price has already been paid in blood.
paras: Having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire. Uncomfortable as the word may sit with a modern man, Paul says that in love God predestined you for adoption. Your salvation was not accomplished by something you did, but by something God did on your behalf — and He did it while you were still in your sin.

Adoption is a legal act, not a sentimental one. It is God placing you in the family with a son’s name, a son’s standing, and a son’s inheritance, according to the good pleasure of his desire — because He wanted to. Not because you qualified.

Then Paul says what it cost. The word behind redemption means to buy back — to purchase a man out of the slave market. You came into this world in your sins; not merely surrounded by them but held by them, needing an intervention from outside yourself. No man can deal with the problem and the consequences of his own sin. The sacrifice of Christ was entirely sufficient to pay the price and buy you back, and when God redeemed you He forgave your debts because they had been paid in full in blood.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: LAVISHED, AND HEADED SOMEWHERE
paras: Verse eight will not let you make God stingy. Paul says grace which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence. God did not merely hand you redemption and forgiveness; He poured them out until they ran over. Whatever else you conclude about the God of this letter, you cannot conclude that He gives grudgingly.

Then Paul lifts your eyes from your own file to the whole of history: God has made known the mystery of His will, to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.

There will be seasons when you cannot tell what God is doing, and seasons when you are tempted to question the way He is doing it. This much is certain: He is bringing all things together under the headship of Jesus Christ, working toward the day when every knee bows and every tongue confesses that He is Lord. Your life is not a loose thread in that. It is being gathered up into it.

So when the dust presses you flat this week and whispers that God has quietly withdrawn, go back to the timestamp and the price. He chose you before the foundation of the world. He adopted you because it pleased Him. He redeemed you with blood and lavished the grace. These blessings are eternal, they are satisfying, and they were never yours to lose.

stations.verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.
stations.question: When I use the word blessed about my own life, am I describing what God has given me in Christ — or reporting on how my circumstances happen to be running?
stations.gloss: worthy of blessing; the One of whom good is spoken
stations.live: Before you ask God for anything this week, give Him one sentence of blessing that has nothing to do with your circumstances: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.’
body: Eulogētos joins eu, well, to logos, word — literally, one well-spoken-of. The etymology matters less than the usage: in the New Testament this exact form is used of God and of no one else. Men receive blessing; God alone is inherently worthy of it.

That settles something men confuse. There is a blessing that comes down and a blessing that goes up, and they are not the same act. God confers; you acknowledge. He blesses by giving; you bless by naming what He gave.
The dust wants your first word about God to be a request. Paul’s first word about God is a doxology, written from a prison cell, before a single petition is filed.

stations.verse: Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love.
stations.question: Do I trace my salvation back to a decision I once made — or to a love the Father set on me before the world had a foundation?
stations.gloss: to pick out for oneself; to choose
stations.live: When accusation comes this week, do not answer it with your recent behavior — you will lose that argument. Answer it with its date: ‘He chose me in Christ before the foundation of the world.’
body: Eklegō means to pick out, to choose. But the decisive thing is the voice. In the New Testament it is always in the middle, which turns the action back on the subject. God did not merely choose. He chose for Himself.

That one detail dismantles the picture most men carry, in which God surveys a field of candidates and takes the promising ones. Jesus put it flatly: You didn’t choose me, but I chose you. God deliberately picks what the world writes off, so no one can boast about the criteria.

The dust argues from your record: look at what you have done. Eklegō answers with a date, not a defense. The choosing happened before the foundation of the world — before there was a record to argue from.

stations.verse: Having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire.
stations.question: Am I living as a servant hoping to be kept on — or as a son whose place in the family was legally settled by someone else?
stations.gloss: adoption; the legal placing of one as a son
stations.live: Name the way you have been living as staff rather than family — the performing, the bracing for dismissal. Then say it back: ‘I was placed in this family by an act of the Father, not by an audition.’
body: Huiothesia joins huios, son, to a form of tithēmi, to place: the placing of a person into the standing of a son. All five New Testament occurrences are Paul’s.

He uses it of Israel’s place among the nations, of the believer’s standing now, and of the redemption of the body still to come (Romans 9:4; 8:15, 23). In every case the weight rests on the will of the Father who adopts, not on the record of the one adopted.

Which is Paul’s point. He predestined you for adoption according to the good pleasure of his desire — not according to your suitability. The dust says you are on probation. Huiothesia says the filing is done, and it was done because it pleased Him.

stations.verse: In whom we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace.
stations.question: Do I still speak of my sin as a weakness to be managed — or as a slavery I had to be bought out of at a price I could never raise?
stations.gloss: release secured by ransom; a buying back out of bondage
stations.live: Take the sin you are most tired of fighting and stop calling it a habit. Call it what Paul calls it — a bondage Christ bought you out of: ‘This was paid for. I am not going back to the market.’
body: Apolytrōsis is built on lytron, the ransom paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war. It does not mean rescue in general, but a specific release, obtained by a specific payment, from a specific bondage. A man in the slave market did not need encouragement. He needed someone with money at the auction.
That is the picture Paul chooses for what God did with your sin. You were not born with unfortunate tendencies. You were born owned — and a slave cannot purchase himself with wages he does not have.

So Paul names the currency: through his blood. The debt was not waived; it was paid in full. That is why this forgiveness is not God overlooking your trespasses but God having settled them. A pardon can be revoked. A purchase cannot be undone.

stations.verse: To an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.
stations.question: When I cannot make sense of what God is doing in the world — or in my own house — do I conclude He has lost the thread, or that He is gathering it?
stations.gloss: to sum up; to gather under one head
stations.live: Name the situation in your life that currently looks like a loose end with no purpose. Do not explain it this week — submit it: ‘You are summing all things up in Christ. Add this in. I will not demand the total early.’
body: Anakephalaioomai appears only twice in the New Testament. Paul uses it in Romans to say the commandments are summed up in one word, love — as a bookkeeper draws a line and writes the total beneath a column. Here it is what God is doing with the universe.

The root is kephalaion, the main point or sum, standing close to kephalē, head. Both senses work at once. God is bringing the scattered totality of things — the heavens, the earth, the years you would rather not revisit — to one total, and the total is a Person.

This answers what a man asks at three in the morning: does any of this go anywhere? The fragments are not loose. They are being gathered toward the fullness of the times — not a hope God entertains but an administration He is running.

practices.title: TAKE THE INVENTORY
practices.body: Write out the eight things Paul says you have in these ten verses — chosen, predestined, adopted, favored, redeemed, forgiven, lavished upon, let in on the mystery. Not a list of what you hope for. A list of what you hold. Read it back to yourself on the worst morning of the week.

practices.title: START WITH THE DOXOLOGY
practices.body: Before you bring God a single request this week, bring Him one sentence of blessing that has nothing to do with your circumstances. Paul writes from prison and the first thing out of him is blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let praise come before petition and see what it does to the petition.

practices.title: ARGUE WITH THE DUST BY DATE
practices.body: When the accusation comes — and it will come with specifics — do not defend yourself with your recent performance. You will lose on the facts. Answer with the timestamp instead: He chose me in Christ before the foundation of the world. An accusation about last week cannot reach a decision made before the world had a foundation.

practices.title: LIVE AT THE PRICE
practices.body: Pick the sin you are most tired of, and stop describing it as a habit. Paul calls it a bondage you were bought out of, at the cost of blood. Say it plainly this week: ‘This was paid for in full. I am not walking back into the market I was purchased out of.’

practices.title: SUBMIT ONE LOOSE END
practices.body: Name the situation you cannot make sense of — the diagnosis, the estranged son, the door that will not open. Do not demand an explanation for it this week. Hand it to the One who is summing all things up in Christ, and let Him keep the column.

title: Blessed Before You Began
subtitle: from dust to every spiritual blessing
keyVerse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.

passage.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ,
even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love,
having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire,
to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved,
in whom we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace,
which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence,
making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him
to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about generating more gratitude by Friday. It is about taking inventory of what is already signed for in your name, and letting a settled blessing steady a man in an unsettled season.
lifePulls: Unlike the temporary blessings this world is chasing, the blessings you have been given in Christ are eternal, satisfying, and glorifying to God — and they were never yours to lose.
prayer: Father, blessed are You, the God and Father of my Lord Jesus Christ. Before I ask You for one thing today, I bless You for what You have already given. You chose me in Christ before the foundation of the world. You adopted me because it pleased You, not because I qualified. You bought me out of my sin with the blood of Your Son, and the debt is paid. When my circumstances turn this week, keep me from reading them as Your verdict. Gather even this day into what You are summing up in Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, blessed are You, the God and Father of my Lord Jesus Christ.
Before I ask You for one thing today, I bless You for what You have already given.
You chose me in Christ before the foundation of the world.
You adopted me because it pleased You, not because I qualified.
You bought me out of my sin with the blood of Your Son, and the debt is paid.
When my circumstances turn this week, keep me from reading them as Your verdict.
Gather even this day into what You are summing up in Christ.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul writes from a prison cell and begins with an inventory, not a complaint: chosen before the foundation of the world, adopted because it pleased the Father, redeemed by blood, forgiven, lavished with grace. Every one of those blessings is stored in the heavenly places, which is why the last twelve months could not touch them. The dust says your standing with God moves with your week. Bless Him first, count what you hold, and stop reading the scoreboard as a verdict.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the scoreboard you have been checking every morning and onto the blessing that was signed before the world had ground to settle on. You did not choose your way into this. You did not qualify for the adoption. You did not raise the ransom, and you are not the one keeping the inheritance safe. Every load-bearing thing in your life with God was set in place before you arrived, and it is held there now by a will that does not waver.

The dust told you that the pressure means God has withdrawn. But look at where Paul is sitting as he writes. A man in chains, whose circumstances have collapsed by every measure the world keeps, opens his letter with the word blessed — and means it about a God who has given him nothing the guards could confiscate. He is not writing you a theory. He is writing you what held him.

So look at the blood. Christ did not shout terms down at you from a safe distance and wait to see whether you could meet them. He came all the way into the low place, into the market where you were held, and paid what you could never raise. That is why your forgiveness is not a mood God is in. It is a purchase He has made, and a purchase does not come undone.

Count it, then, even while the season is hard. Chosen. Adopted. Redeemed. Forgiven. Lavished upon. And gathered — with everything else in heaven and on earth — under the headship of Jesus Christ, who is summing up all things and has not lost the thread of yours. Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to, and stand up as a man who has already been blessed with every spiritual blessing.
closingVerse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.
carry: Where have you been reading your circumstances as God’s current verdict on you — when Paul would have you read them as weather passing over a blessing that was settled before the foundation of the world?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a species of doubt that does not attack God. It attacks the paperwork. A man can hold a high view of Christ, believe every word of the creed, and still lie awake at two in the morning running the same audit: did it take? He is not questioning whether the gospel is true. He is questioning whether it is true of him.

That audit has no end, because it has no fixed reference point. It reads the evidence off your own performance, and your performance moves. A good week produces assurance; a bad week withdraws it. And a man who lives that way will eventually conclude the very thing Paul is writing to make impossible — that his standing with God is provisional, pending review.

The dust tells you that assurance is something you generate, and that the way to get more of it is to try harder and feel more. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul worn out by that arithmetic: my soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) And the reviving word of this passage is that God did not leave your assurance to your own bookkeeping. He put a seal on you.

sections.heading: How a Man Is Actually Saved
pulls: The dust says your standing with God is provisional, pending review. Ephesians 1 says a seal was applied the day you believed — and a seal is not a mood. It is a mark of ownership.
paras: This passage is one of the most concise explanations in all of Scripture of what happened to you when God saved you from your sin through the finished work of Christ. Watch the order Paul gives, because the order matters.

First, you heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation. The gospel has to be heard. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, and the gospel is the power of God for salvation — which means it must reach a man’s ears before it can reach his heart. Second, you believed. Not worked, not earned, not qualified: believed. A man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Third, and only then, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

Notice that the sealing is not something you achieved after a long apprenticeship. It is not a second blessing you pray your way into or a reward for the spiritually advanced. It is what God does to a man the moment he believes.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: AN INHERITANCE ASSIGNED, NOT EARNED
paras: Paul begins by saying that we were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will. How did you obtain this inheritance? Not by accumulation. By assignment. It was allotted to you, the way land was allotted to the tribes — by a decision made somewhere above you and before you.

And look at the reach of the clause Paul attaches: him who does all things after the counsel of his will. Not some things. All things. The same God who assigned your inheritance is running the whole board, which means the events that look to you like interference are inside the same counsel that guaranteed the inheritance in the first place.

Paul says the purpose of all of it is that we should be to the praise of his glory — a phrase he repeats three times in this chapter like a man striking the same nail. Your salvation terminates on God’s glory, not on your comfort. That sounds severe until you realize what it secures: a salvation resting on God’s commitment to His own name is infinitely safer than one resting on His commitment to your usefulness.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: SEALED, AND HELD AS A DOWN PAYMENT
paras: Then comes the sealing, and Paul immediately explains what the seal is for. The Spirit is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession. A pledge is a first installment — money down that legally obligates the buyer to complete the purchase.

So the presence of the Spirit in your life is not something you earn or work up. He is the gift by which God has marked you as His, and He is the guarantee of everything still owed to you. This is why assurance is not a feeling you manufacture. The seal was applied by Someone else, and the down payment sits in God’s account, not yours.

And notice the direction of the guarantee. The Spirit does not guarantee that your circumstances will improve. He guarantees the inheritance — which means the worst thing that can happen to you in this life cannot reach the thing that has been promised to you in the next.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: A PRAYER WORTH LEARNING
pulls: Paul does not pray for relief. He prays that the eyes of their hearts would be opened — because a man who sees what he already has can survive almost anything.
paras: Paul then tells them how he prays, and it is worth noticing what he does not ask for. He has heard of their faith and their love, and he does not cease to give thanks and to make mention of them.

But when he comes to petition, he does not ask for easier circumstances. He asks for a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, and for the eyes of your hearts enlightened, so they would know three things: the hope of His calling, the riches of the glory of His inheritance, and the exceeding greatness of His power toward those who believe.

You encounter people every day who need prayer, and most of what comes out of you is well-meant repetition — better circumstances, improved relationships, relief. It rarely gets anywhere near the actual problem. It rarely goes deep enough to be scriptural.

Imagine what would change if you memorized these verses and prayed them for the people in front of you. Not give him a break but open the eyes of his heart. There are men in your circle just as desperate for the power of God as you are for it in yourself.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE POWER THAT RAISED HIM
paras: Then Paul does something you would not expect. He needs a measurement for God’s power toward believers, and the only unit large enough is the resurrection. That power is according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places.

The same energy that emptied the tomb is the energy at work toward you. Not a lesser grade of it. The same. And the Christ it raised is now seated far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, with all things in subjection under His feet — and given to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

Read that last phrase slowly. Christ’s universal supremacy is exercised for the church. He is not merely above everything; He is above everything on behalf of His people. So when the dust tells you that you are unnoticed and provisional, answer it with the seal and the throne. You were marked the day you believed, the deposit is already paid, and the One holding it is seated over every power that could possibly threaten you.

stations.verse: We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will.
stations.question: Do I think of my place in Christ as something I have been building — or as something that was allotted to me before I could contribute anything to it?
stations.gloss: to assign by lot; to appoint a portion
stations.live: Name the thing you are trying hardest to earn from God this week — approval, usefulness, a sense of being wanted. Then set it down and say: ‘My portion was assigned, not won.’
body: Klēroō comes from klēros, a lot — the marker cast to settle a decision. In the New Testament the verb appears only here. It is the picture of Joshua dividing the land by the lot of their inheritance: no tribe negotiated its portion, and no tribe earned it. The allotment came from outside.

Paul uses that word for what happened to you. Your share in Christ was not accumulated over years of faithfulness; it was assigned. And in Scripture the lot was never random — the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh.

The dust wants your inheritance to feel like something you are still qualifying for, so that every failure threatens it. Klēroō says the distribution is finished. Your name is already written beside a portion you did nothing to deserve.

stations.verse: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation — in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
stations.question: When I look for evidence that I belong to God, do I look at my own performance — or at what He did to me the day I believed?
stations.gloss: to seal; to stamp with a mark of ownership
stations.live: When the two-in-the-morning audit begins this week, stop the accounting and say one sentence: ‘I was sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. The mark is His, not mine, and it was pressed in before I had a record to defend.’
body: Sphragizō means to set a seal on something — to mark it as belonging to someone. Scripture uses the seal that way: God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are his.”
Paul says God did that to you with the Holy Spirit. Not with an emotion, not with a track record — with a Person. The seal is not evidence you produce; it is a mark Someone else applied.

And notice the timing: having also believed, you were sealed. Not after a probationary period. The dust will let you spend a lifetime hunting for proof you are His. The proof was pressed into you the day you believed.

stations.verse: Who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.
stations.question: Am I living as though my future with God were still uncertain — or as though a deposit had already been paid against it?
stations.gloss: a down payment; earnest money guaranteeing the rest
stations.live: Take one comfort of the Spirit you have actually known this week — a moment of peace, conviction, or steadiness — and name it out loud as what it is: ‘That was the first installment, not the whole sum.’
body: Arrabōn is a Semitic word carried into Greek — the Greek Old Testament uses it for the pledge Judah left with Tamar — and it means the first installment on a purchase. It is not a gift or a token. It is money down of the same kind as the balance, legally binding the buyer to complete the transaction.

So when Paul calls the Spirit an arrabōn, he is saying the Spirit is not a substitute for glory but a piece of it, paid in advance. What you experience of God now is the same currency as what is coming, only in a smaller amount.

The dust says heaven is a hope you are talking yourself into. Arrabōn answers that the down payment has cleared. God has bound Himself to finish what He has begun, and the guarantee is not a promise in a book — it is a Person living in you.

stations.verse: Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.
stations.question: What would change in my week if I stopped asking God to alter my circumstances and started asking Him to open my eyes?
stations.gloss: to give light; to bring into view what was already there
stations.live: Pray Paul’s prayer this week for one person by name, word for word, instead of praying for their circumstances. Then pray it for yourself before you ask God for anything else.
body: Phōtizō means to illuminate. The important thing about illumination is what it does not do: it does not create the room. Light adds nothing to the furniture. It only makes visible what was already standing there in the dark.

That is precisely Paul’s request. He does not pray that God would give them a hope, riches, and power they lack. He prays that the eyes of their hearts would be lit so they can see what they already possess.

That changes how you pray. The dust tells a struggling man that he needs more from God. Paul suggests he may first need to see what he has already been given — and that the seeing itself is a work only God can do.

stations.verse: He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly.
stations.question: Do I believe Christ reigns over everything in general — or that He reigns over everything specifically on behalf of His people, including me?
stations.gloss: head; the source and authority over a body
stations.live: Name the power that most intimidates you right now — an institution, a diagnosis, a person who holds your job in his hand. Then place it where Paul places it: ‘That is under His feet, and He is head over it for me.’
body: Kephalē carries both authority and organic connection. A head rules a body, but it is also the same living thing as the body — you cannot injure one without the other feeling it. Paul will use the word again to say the church grows up into Christ.

But the decisive word in this verse is the little preposition: God gave Him to be head over all things for the assembly. Christ’s supremacy is not neutral. It is exercised on behalf of a particular people.

The dust says the powers running the world have no interest in you and no one is holding them. Paul says every rule, authority, power, and dominion is already under His feet, and the One whose feet they are under is joined to you as a head to a body.

practices.title: STOP THE AUDIT
practices.body: When the two-in-the-morning review begins, do not answer it with evidence from your week. Answer it with the sealing: having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit. The mark was applied by God, on the day you believed, and no bad month has authority to lift it.

practices.title: TRACE THE ORDER
practices.body: Write down the three steps Paul gives — heard, believed, sealed. Then locate yourself honestly in that order. Most men who doubt their salvation are looking for a fourth step that Paul never wrote, and exhausting themselves trying to reach it.

practices.title: PRAY THE PASSAGE FOR ONE MAN
practices.body: Pick one person this week and pray verses seventeen through nineteen for him by name, word for word. Not better circumstances. Enlightened eyes, the hope of his calling, the riches of the inheritance, the greatness of the power. Then notice how different that is from what you usually pray.

practices.title: NAME THE DEPOSIT
practices.body: Identify one thing the Spirit has actually done in you — a conviction you could not have produced, a peace that arrived from outside. Call it what Paul calls it: earnest money. The first installment of an inheritance God has legally bound Himself to pay in full.

practices.title: PUT THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS
practices.body: Name the thing that intimidates you most this week, and then say where it sits: under His feet. Christ is head over all things for the church. His supremacy is not a distant fact; it is exercised on behalf of the body you belong to.

title: Sealed and Not Forgotten
subtitle: from dust to a guaranteed inheritance
keyVerse: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation — in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

passage.text: We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will,
to the end that we should be to the praise of his glory, we who had before hoped in Christ.
In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,
who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.
For this cause I also, having heard of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you, and the love which you have toward all the saints,
don’t cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers,
that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him,
having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might
which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places,
far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come.
He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly,
which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about working up more certainty. It is about resting on a seal you did not apply and a deposit you did not pay, and learning to pray for others the way Paul prayed.
lifePulls: The presence of the Spirit is not something you earn or pray your way into. He is the gift by which God marked you as His — and the guarantee of everything still owed to you.
prayer: Father, I heard the word of truth, and I believed, and You sealed me with Your Spirit. I confess I keep auditing my own week for proof that I am Yours. Your mark is on me, and I did not put it there. Thank You for the down payment of Your Spirit, and for the inheritance He guarantees. Open the eyes of my heart to the hope of Your calling and the riches I already hold. Show me the power that raised Christ and seated Him far above every name. Teach me to pray that prayer for the men around me, not only for their circumstances. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I heard the word of truth, and I believed, and You sealed me with Your Spirit.
I confess I keep auditing my own week for proof that I am Yours.
Your mark is on me, and I did not put it there.
Thank You for the down payment of Your Spirit, and for the inheritance He guarantees.
Open the eyes of my heart to the hope of Your calling and the riches I already hold.
Show me the power that raised Christ and seated Him far above every name.
Teach me to pray that prayer for the men around me, not only for their
circumstances.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: You heard the word of truth, you believed, and God sealed you with the promised Holy Spirit — a mark of ownership and a down payment on everything still owed you. Assurance is not something you generate on a good week; it was pressed into you the day you believed. So Paul does not pray for relief. He prays for opened eyes, because a man who sees what he already holds in the risen Christ can endure almost anything.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the ledger you have been keeping on yourself and onto the seal you did not apply. You did not earn the inheritance; it was assigned. You did not pay the deposit; it was made on your behalf. You did not press the mark into your own life; God did that with His own Spirit on the day you first believed the Good News of your salvation.

The dust told you that your standing is provisional and under review. But a seal is not a mood, and a down payment is not a hope. In the world Paul was writing to, a seal on a jar meant somebody owned it, it was genuine, and no one else could open it. That is what God did to you. You are owned, you are authenticated, and you are closed against every hand that would tamper with what belongs to Him.

So look where Christ is sitting. Not waiting to see how your week goes, but seated at the right hand of the Father, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion and every name that is named — in this age and in the age still coming. Every force that has ever made you feel small is already under His feet. And He holds that position, Paul says, for the assembly — for the body you were joined to when you believed.

Pray, then, for opened eyes rather than easier days. Ask Him to light the room you are already standing in, so you can see the hope of His calling, the riches of the glory of His inheritance, and the exceeding greatness of His power toward those who believe. There are men in your circle just as desperate for that as you are. Lift your eyes off the ledger, and look at the seal God pressed into you.
closingVerse: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation — in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
carry: Where have you been hunting for proof that you belong to God — when Paul would have you look instead at the mark He pressed into you the day you believed, and at the down payment already sitting in His account?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Chapter one told you what God is doing in this world: bringing all things in heaven and on earth into subjection to Christ, until every knee bows and every tongue confesses that He is Lord. Chapter two tells you how He is accomplishing it. And the plan begins in a graveyard.

That is not a figure of speech Paul reaches for casually. He could have said you were weak, misguided, unfulfilled, or off course. He says you were dead in transgressions and sins. This is the bluntest diagnosis of the human condition anywhere in his letters, and it is the reason every program of self-improvement ever devised has missed the actual problem.

The dust tells you that your trouble is a matter of degree — that you were running low, and grace topped you off. It lets you keep a little credit for the turnaround. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man who has finally stopped pretending: my soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) And the reviving word of Ephesians 2 is that you did not improve. You were raised.

sections.heading: What the Fall Actually Cost
pulls: The dust lets you believe you were running low and grace topped you off. Paul says you were in a grave. Corpses do not need encouragement. They need a resurrection.
paras: You will see from this passage just how devastating the fall in the garden actually was. God had warned Adam concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil that in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die. Physical death was the long-term result. Spiritual death was immediate. As soon as they ate, their eyes were opened, their nakedness was exposed, and the next time God came walking, they hid.

And that decision did not stay with them. Sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; so death passed to all men, because all sinned. Which is why Paul can write to living, breathing, working people in Ephesus and say you were dead. If anything spiritual was going to happen in anyone’s life, they would first have to be raised. It is the same thing Jesus told a religious man who had everything else in order: You must be born anew.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THREE THINGS TRUE OF A MAN WITHOUT CHRIST
paras: Being dead is not the only bad news in these verses. Paul says the dead also walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience. In other words, a man outside of Christ is not neutral and he is not independent. He is under influence — moving with a current he did not choose and mostly cannot see.

Then comes the third thing, and it is the hardest: outside of Christ you were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. Not children of wrath by accident or by an unusually bad stretch, but by nature. The problem was never simply what you did. It was what you were.
Dead, under the influence of the evil one, and by nature children of wrath. That is the honest inventory, and there is no verse in this passage that softens it. But there is a verse that answers it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: BUT GOD
paras: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ. Two words turn the whole letter, and they are not two words about you.

Notice the timing: even when we were dead. Not after you showed promise. Not once you had begun to stir. God did not wait for a flicker of life to justify His intervention, because there was none to wait for. Dead men cannot raise themselves, so God did it for them in Christ.

And notice the two attributes Paul names as the cause. Mercy — and He is rich in it, not rationing it. And love — his great love with which he loved us. Your salvation did not originate in anything attractive about you. It originated in something inexhaustible about Him.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: RAISED, AND SEATED
pulls: Being made alive would have been mercy enough. He seated you — and a seated man is a man whose standing is no longer under review.
paras: Then Paul says where God put you. He raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. Being made alive would have been mercy enough. Being seated is something else entirely.

A man who is seated is a man who is no longer under review. Hebrews says Christ sat down on the right hand of God once His one sacrifice was offered. A seat means the work is done. Paul says your seat is not a future arrangement but a present location — in Christ Jesus, in the same heavenly places where chapter one told you your blessings are stored and where chapter six will tell you the real war is fought.

And God did it, Paul says, that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us. You are exhibit evidence. For all eternity God intends to point at people He raised out of the dust as the demonstration of what His grace is like.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: GRACE, FAITH, AND THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS
paras: So Paul states it plainly: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast. Salvation from sin is a gracious gift, not something earned, merited, or deserved. Do you want to understand how you were saved? Do not look at yourself. Look at the free grace God has given you in Christ.

You were not saved by the work of your hands but through the instrument of trust. You simply trusted God. By His grace He enabled you to throw your hands up and say: Lord, there is nothing I can do to save myself. Have mercy and save.

And then verse ten, which men who love grace sometimes skip: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. Works are not the root of your salvation. They are the fruit of it. God did not raise you out of the dust to leave you sitting in the corner; He prepared a path in advance and then made you the kind of man who could walk it.
Take time this week to thank God that He has done for you what you could not do for yourself. Even though you were dead in trespasses and sins, He has made you alive by grace through faith.

stations.verse: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins.
stations.question: Do I describe my life before Christ as misguided and struggling — or as Paul describes it, dead and past helping myself?
stations.gloss: dead; a corpse, without capacity to respond
stations.live: Say the honest version out loud this week: ‘I was not struggling. I was dead, and I did not raise myself.’ Then notice how much lighter it is to stop defending a contribution you never made.
body: Nekros is the ordinary Greek word for a dead body. It is not a metaphor for low energy or poor decisions. Paul had every milder word available to him — weak, sick, lost, straying — and he chose the one that describes a corpse.

That choice decides everything downstream. A sick man needs medicine and a lost man needs directions, but both can still cooperate. A dead man contributes nothing at all. He cannot want to be raised, cannot ask, cannot begin.
The dust prefers the milder words, because each of them leaves you a little credit for the recovery. Nekros leaves you none. Which is exactly why the next thing Paul says is not about you at all.

stations.verse: We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.
stations.question: Do I treat my sin as a series of bad choices — or as the expression of a nature I was born with and could not reform?
stations.gloss: nature; what a thing is by birth rather than by choice
stations.live: Take the sin you keep managing rather than confessing. Stop treating it as a policy failure this week and take it to God as evidence of what you are apart from Him.
body: Physis means the constitution a thing has by origin — what it is before it does anything. Paul is not saying you became a child of wrath by behaving badly enough. He is saying you were one by birth.
This is the difference between a man who tells lies and a liar. Behavior can be corrected by pressure; nature cannot. And a nature is not something a man can step outside of long enough to repair.

The dust will always steer you toward the behavioral account, because behavior is manageable and nature is not. But Paul’s diagnosis is the reason his cure is so radical. God did not reform the old nature. He made you alive together with Christ.

stations.verse: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us.
stations.question: When I think of God’s mercy toward me, do I picture it as carefully measured — or as the wealth of Someone who cannot run short?
stations.gloss: rich; abounding in resources
stations.live: Name the sin you assume has finally exhausted God’s patience. Then set it beside the word rich and ask honestly whether your account of Him has been too small.
body: Plousios is the ordinary word for a wealthy man, and Paul applies it to God’s mercy. The point is not that God is merciful but that He is rich in it — that mercy is not something He is running low on and dispensing carefully.

Wealth vocabulary runs all through this letter: the riches of His grace, the riches of the glory of His inheritance, the unsearchable riches of Christ. Paul keeps reaching for it because a suffering church needs to know that the supply is not the problem.

The dust rations. It tells you that you have used up your share, that this failure was the one that finally cost you. Plousios answers that a rich man is not diminished by giving, and God has never once had to check the balance before showing mercy.

stations.verse: And raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Am I living like a man still auditioning for his place — or like a man who has already been seated?
stations.gloss: to seat together with; to be enthroned alongside
stations.live: Notice where you are still standing before God this week — still explaining, still proving. Then take the seat: ‘I am not on trial here. I was seated with Christ.’
body: Sygkathizō joins syn, together with, to kathizō, to seat. Paul builds three of these compounds in a row — made alive with, raised with, seated with — hammering the same prefix so no one misses that none of it happened to you alone.

And the tense matters. Paul does not say God will seat you. He says He did. Hebrews makes the same point: every priest stands day by day, but Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God. Sitting is the posture of finished work.

The dust keeps you on your feet, always presenting, always waiting for the verdict. Sygkathizō says the verdict came in, the seat was assigned, and the One you are seated with is the One every power in this letter is under.

stations.verse: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
stations.question: Do I do good work to secure God’s approval — or because He made me for it and laid the path out ahead of time?
stations.gloss: something made; a work of craftsmanship
stations.live: Before you plan your week, ask a different question than usual: not ‘what should I accomplish for God’ but ‘what has He already prepared for me to walk in today?’
body: Poiēma appears only twice in the New Testament. Paul’s other use is in Romans, where it describes the created world as the thing God made. Here he uses the same word for you.

It is a maker’s word, and it settles the question of who the active party is. A piece of work does not commission itself. And Paul adds that the good works themselves were prepared before — laid out in advance, so that walking in them is following a path rather than inventing one.

The dust tells a man his usefulness is his justification, and then keeps raising the standard. Poiēma reverses the order. You are not working to become God’s workmanship. You are His workmanship, and that is why you can work at all.

practices.title: LET THE DIAGNOSIS STAND
practices.body: Read verses one through three without softening them. Do not translate dead into struggling. Sit with the full inventory — dead, under the influence of the prince of the power of the air, by nature a child of wrath — and resist the urge to argue for partial credit. Nothing makes grace smaller than a diagnosis that has been negotiated down.

practices.title: UNDERLINE THE TWO WORDS
practices.body: Find the words But God in verse four and mark them in your Bible. Everything before them is your condition and everything after them is His work. When the accusation comes this week, do not start your defense at verse one. Start it at verse four.

practices.title: TAKE THE SEAT
practices.body: Notice where you are still standing before God — still explaining yourself, still presenting evidence, still waiting to hear whether you are approved. Then say what Paul says: God raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places. A seated man is not on trial.

practices.title: STOP RATIONING HIS MERCY
practices.body: Name the failure you assume has finally used up God’s patience. Then set it beside the word Paul chose — rich in mercy. A wealthy man is not diminished by what he gives away, and God has never yet had to check the balance before He forgave you.

practices.title: WALK THE PATH ALREADY LAID
practices.body: Before you plan your week, ask what God has prepared rather than what you should achieve. You are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works He laid out beforehand. Your job this week is not to invent a path. It is to walk in one.

title: Dead in the Dust, Alive in Christ
subtitle: from dust to the heavenly places
keyVerse: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved.

passage.text: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins,
in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience.
We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.
But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus;
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is not about trying to feel more grateful. It is about letting the honest diagnosis stand — dead, influenced, by nature a child of wrath — so that the two words that answer it can finally land with their full weight.
lifePulls: You were not saved by the work of your hands but through the instrument of trust. By His grace He enabled you to throw your hands up and say: Lord, there is nothing I can do to save myself.
prayer: Father, I was dead in my trespasses and sins, and I did not raise myself. I followed the course of this world and called it freedom. But You, rich in mercy, made me alive together with Christ. You raised me with Him and seated me with Him, and I am not on trial today. Keep me from taking credit for any part of Your work. Thank You that even my faith was Your gift. Show me the good works You prepared beforehand, and give me the will to walk in them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I was dead in my trespasses and sins, and I did not raise myself.
I followed the course of this world and called it freedom.
But You, rich in mercy, made me alive together with Christ.
You raised me with Him and seated me with Him, and I am not on trial today.
Keep me from taking credit for any part of Your work.
Thank You that even my faith was Your gift.
Show me the good works You prepared beforehand, and give me the will to walk in them.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul’s diagnosis is the bluntest in Scripture: dead in trespasses and sins, following the course of this world, by nature a child of wrath. Then come two words that have nothing to do with you — But God. Rich in mercy, He made you alive with Christ while you were still dead, raised you, and seated you with Him. Salvation is by grace through faith, the faith itself is His gift, and the good works come after, prepared beforehand so a raised man has somewhere to walk.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the ground where you were lying and onto the God who came down to it. You were not weak; you were dead. You were not merely off course; you were walking with a current you could not see, in a nature you did not choose and could not repair. That is the honest reading of what you were, and there is not a verse in this chapter that softens it.

But look at what stands in the middle of the sentence. But God. Two words, and they are not about you at all. He was rich in mercy when you had none to appeal to. He loved you with His own great love while you were still dead in your trespasses. He did not wait at the edge of the grave for you to stir. He came in and made you alive together with Christ, because that is the only way a dead man has ever been helped.

And He did not leave you standing at the graveside blinking in the light. He raised you up with Him and seated you with Him in the heavenly places — the same heavenly places where your blessings are stored and where every power that frightens you is already under His feet. You are not on trial. You are not auditioning for a place you already occupy. Christ sat down when His work was finished, and you are seated with Him.

So walk. Not to earn the seat, but because you have one. You are His workmanship, and the works were prepared before you ever thought to look for them, which means the path in front of you this week was laid by the same hands that raised you. Lift your eyes off the dust of what you were, and go walk in what He has made you.
closingVerse: But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved.
carry: Where have you been quietly negotiating the diagnosis down — calling yourself struggling rather than dead — and so leaving yourself a little credit that makes the words but God smaller than they are?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Throughout this letter Paul refers to the Jews as we and the Gentiles as you. He was a Jew by birth and a self-described Pharisee of Pharisees, and God had specifically called him to carry the gospel to the Gentiles. The church at Ephesus was mostly Gentile with Jews scattered throughout, and Paul understood that the unity between them would not be achieved by good manners. It would require a death.

So he begins by making them remember. Remember that you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world. Five phrases, each one taking something away, until nothing is left standing.

The dust tells you that you are on the outside of something — that the real Christians, the settled families, the men who grew up in it, belong in a way you never quite will. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man who has been circling a house he does not believe he is welcome in: my soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) And the reviving word of Ephesians 2 is that the distance was closed from the other side, in blood.

sections.heading: A Work Done Through His Church
pulls: The dust tells you that you are circling a house you do not belong in. Ephesians 2 says the distance was closed from the other side, and closed in blood.
paras: It is important to see that the work God is doing in this world will be accomplished through His church. God has chosen to use His people, through His word, directed by His Spirit, to take His gospel to the four corners of the earth. You are part of that plan. You have a place in it, and it should be your ambition to play your role in it.

Which is why the barrier between Jew and Gentile mattered so much to Paul, and why the barriers you tolerate matter now. A divided church is a contradicted gospel. Christ prayed that His people would be one, that the world may know that the Father sent Him. The unity of the body is not a nice feature of the Christian life. It is evidence.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: REMEMBER WHAT YOU WERE
paras: Paul calls them the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision. Notice how carefully he handles it. The labels were being thrown around as insults, and Paul does not pretend otherwise — but he adds in the flesh, made by hands, which quietly empties the insult of its authority.

Then he lists what was actually true. Separate from Christ. Alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. Strangers from the covenants of the promise. Having no hope. Without God in the world. That is not exclusion from a club; that is exclusion from every promise God had ever made.

Paul makes them remember it, and he is not being cruel. A man who has forgotten how far off he was will always underestimate what it cost to bring him near — and will always be harder on the people still standing where he used to stand.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE WALL CAME DOWN IN HIS FLESH
paras: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation. Paul knew what that wall had cost. Acts records that he was nearly killed in Jerusalem because a crowd supposed that Paul had brought Trophimus, an Ephesian, into the temple.

And notice what Paul says Christ did with it. He did not open a gate in it. He broke it down, having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances. The ceremonial system that had marked the separation was fulfilled and therefore finished, and it was finished in a body on a cross.

The purpose was constructive, not merely demolition: that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace, and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it. Not Gentiles absorbed into Judaism, and not Jews absorbed into Gentile culture. Something new, made in Christ, that did not exist before.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: PEACE PREACHED, ACCESS GIVEN
pulls: He did not open a gate in the wall. He broke it down — and He did it in His own flesh, so that what stood between you and God is now a ruin behind you.
paras: Then Paul says something worth slowing down for: He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near. Christ did not send peace by messenger. He came and preached it Himself, and He preached it to both groups — because both needed it, though only one of them had known it.

And the result is through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father. One access, one Spirit, one Father. The Trinity is in that sentence, and so is the end of every claim any man could make to a shorter route in.

You are now part of the body of Christ. There are many denominations in the world, but there is really only one church, and Christ is the head of it. God has not given each congregation a separate mission. He has given every one of His people the same commission — to go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them to observe all He commanded. And to do it you must, as far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Now that God has made peace with you through the blood of Christ, pursue peace with others, especially those of the household of faith.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: CITIZENS, FAMILY, AND A TEMPLE STILL RISING
paras: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God. Paul changes the metaphor twice in one sentence. Citizenship gives you standing; household gives you belonging. He wants both, because a man can be legally admitted somewhere and still eat alone.

Then the picture becomes architectural. You are built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. The foundation from which you live was not laid by your earthly family. It was laid by the apostles and prophets and by Christ Himself.

And the building is not finished. It grows — a strange verb for masonry, and Paul means it. God is still fitting stones together, and in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit. The temple He is raising is not a place you visit. It is a people you are being set into.

You cannot read this passage and walk away with a lone-ranger faith. God did not save you to fix your life and make you comfortable. He saved you to extend His mercy to you and to make you part of the work He is doing through His church. You who were once dead are now of the household of God. You who once walked according to the course of this world are now led by His Spirit. You who were by nature a child of wrath are now at peace with God, brought near by the blood of Christ.

stations.verse: That you were at that time separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
stations.question: Have I forgotten how far off I actually was — and has forgetting made me harder on people who are still standing there?
stations.gloss: to be alienated; made a stranger to what one had no claim on
stations.live: Write down honestly what you were before Christ — not a softened version. Then read verse thirteen aloud over it and let but now do its work.
body: Apallotrioō is built on allotrios, belonging to another. To be alienated in this sense is not to have been thrown out of something that was yours. It is to stand outside something that was never yours to begin with. Paul stacks five deprivations here, and the last is the heaviest: without God in the world. Not without religion. The Ephesians had a great deal of religion and a temple famous across the empire. Without God.

The dust works both directions with this memory. It either erases it, so that grace feels ordinary, or it weaponizes it, so that a man cannot believe he was truly brought in. Paul’s cure for both is the same: remember accurately, then read the next verse.

stations.verse: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.
stations.question: When I feel distant from God, do I try to close the gap with effort — or remember who already closed it, and at what cost?
stations.gloss: near; at hand, in close proximity
stations.live: The next time distance from God is what you feel, do not try to feel your way back. Say instead: ‘I was made near in the blood of Christ, and that has not changed since Friday.’
body: Engys is a word of physical proximity, and in Israel’s worship it was intensely practical. Nearness to God was measured in courts and curtains, and the closer you were permitted to come, the greater the qualification required.

Paul says the far-off have been made near — a passive verb, something done to them — and he names the means: in the blood of Christ. Not by improved behavior, not by adopting the customs of the near, but by a death.
The dust measures your nearness to God by how close you feel this morning. Engys measures it by where the blood has placed you. Feelings move; the placement does not.

stations.verse: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.
stations.question: What wall am I still maintaining that Christ has already torn down — and what does it cost the church that I keep it standing?
stations.gloss: a middle wall; a partition dividing a space
stations.live: Name one line you quietly maintain — by background, politics, income, or history — between yourself and other believers. Ask God this week to show you why you are still guarding a ruin.
body: Mesotoichos occurs only here in the New Testament, and it is a builder’s word — mesos, middle, joined to toichos, wall. Acts shows how real such a wall was: Paul was nearly killed in Jerusalem because a crowd supposed that Paul had brought Trophimus, an Ephesian, into the temple.
The verb matters as much as the noun. Christ did not install a gate or grant exceptions. He broke it down, and Paul says He did it in his flesh — the demolition happened in a body, on a cross.

The dust rebuilds. It is remarkable how quickly a people who were brought in by pure mercy begin drawing lines around the room. Every wall you maintain in the church is masonry Christ has already pulled down.

stations.verse: For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.
stations.question: Do I come to God as one who has been granted an audience — or as though I still need to arrange my own introduction?
stations.gloss: access; being brought into a royal presence
stations.live: Begin one prayer this week without any preamble of self-justification. No explaining your week first. Come in the way Paul says you come: escorted, in one Spirit, to the Father.
body: Prosagōgē comes from prosagō, to bring to, and means approach or access. The word carries the sense of being brought: nobody wandered into a throne room, and the one who brought you in vouched for you with his own standing.

That is why Paul says through him. Christ is not merely the reason access exists; He is the One who conducts you in. And the access is in one Spirit to the Father — all three Persons in a single short line.
The dust makes you arrange your own introduction, rehearsing until you sound presentable enough to be admitted. Prosagōgē says you were brought in by Someone whose welcome is not in question.

stations.verse: In whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.
stations.question: Do I treat the church as a service I attend — or as the building God is actually raising, with me set into the wall?
stations.gloss: to build together into one structure
stations.live: Identify one place you have kept yourself structurally separate from your church — attending without bearing weight. Take on one load this week that someone else would otherwise carry.
body: Synoikodomeō is another of Paul’s syn- compounds: built together. It appears only here in the New Testament. In this short passage he also uses fitted together and grows, all describing a structure assembled from parts that were never designed to stand alone.

A stone in a wall has no independent function. Its strength is entirely in its placement and in the stones it bears against. Paul chooses that image deliberately for people who had just been told they were far off.

The dust prefers a private faith with no one close enough to notice the cracks. Synoikodomeō says God is not building a collection of separate monuments. He is raising one habitation, and you are load-bearing in it.

practices.title: REMEMBER ACCURATELY
practices.body: Write down what you actually were before Christ, using Paul’s five phrases as the template — separate, alienated, a stranger, without hope, without God. Do not soften it. A man who forgets how far off he was will always underestimate the blood and overestimate himself.

practices.title: READ BUT NOW OVER IT
practices.body: Then read verse thirteen aloud over that list. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ. Your nearness to God is not a reading you take each morning off your own feelings. It is a placement, and it was purchased.

practices.title: FIND THE WALL YOU ARE GUARDING
practices.body: Name one line you quietly maintain between yourself and other believers — background, politics, income, history, the way they worship. Christ broke that wall down in His own flesh. Ask God this week why you are still standing watch over a ruin.

practices.title: COME IN WITHOUT PREAMBLE
practices.body: Begin one prayer this week with no self-justification in front of it. No summary of how the week went, no case for why you should be heard. You have access through Christ, in one Spirit, to the Father. Walk in as a man who has been escorted.

practices.title: BEAR SOME WEIGHT
practices.body: You are built together into a habitation of God, and a stone in a wall carries load. Find one thing in your church this week that someone else is carrying alone, and take it. Attendance is not placement.

title: Brought Near by Blood
subtitle: from dust to the household of God
keyVerse: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.

passage.text: Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called “uncircumcision” by that which is called “circumcision” (in the flesh, made by hands),
that you were at that time separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.
He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.
For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.
So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,
being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone;
in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly — and where a Greek word is opened up, let it sharpen the verse you have just prayed over.
lifeIntro: This week is about two things Paul refuses to separate: what it cost to bring you near, and what that nearness obligates you to toward the people He brought near alongside you.
lifePulls: God did not save you to fix your life and make you comfortable. He saved you to extend His mercy to you and to make you part of the work He is doing through His church.
prayer: Father, I was far off — without Christ, without hope, without You in the world. You did not wait for me to close the distance. You brought me near in the blood of Your Son, who is our peace. Thank You that I come to You through Christ, in one Spirit, and not by my own introduction. Show me the wall I am still guarding between myself and Your people. Tear it down in me, the way Christ tore it down in His flesh. Fit me into Your household, and let me carry weight there. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I was far off — without Christ, without hope, without You in the world.
You did not wait for me to close the distance.
You brought me near in the blood of Your Son, who is our peace.
Thank You that I come to You through Christ, in one Spirit, and not by my own introduction.
Show me the wall I am still guarding between myself and Your people.
Tear it down in me, the way Christ tore it down in His flesh.
Fit me into Your household, and let me carry weight there.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: You were far off — separate from Christ, alienated from Israel, a stranger to the covenants, without hope and without God. Then Paul writes But now. The distance was closed in the blood of Christ, who broke down the middle wall in His own flesh and made one new man out of two. You are no longer a stranger but a member of the household, a stone being fitted into a temple that is still rising.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the doorstep you have been sitting on and onto the house you have already been brought inside. You were far off — not distant in mood but genuinely outside, with no claim on a single promise God had ever made. Paul does not let you forget it, and he is not being cruel. He knows that a man who forgets the distance will always misprice the blood.

But look what stands between what you were and what you are. But now in Christ Jesus. Not but now that you have grown. Not but now that you have proven steady.
